messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 33-year-old Ghanaian-born tailor who has been living in the United States for six years. He came to the country with a clear sense of direction — to build a small alterations and custom-clothing business — and for a time, that plan was unfolding steadily. He rented a modest shop space, built a loyal clientele, and carried himself with the quiet pride of a craftsman who knew his work was good. That version of his life ended on an afternoon eighteen months ago, when he was visiting a busy open-air market in the city where his cousin lived, attending what was meant to be a cultural festival. A bomb detonated near the main stage. Kofi was approximately forty feet away when the blast occurred. He remembered the sound before the pressure — a crack that seemed to split the air itself — and then the ground, and smoke, and the screaming of people he could not see. He recalled running toward an exit along a chain-link fence, pressing through a crowd that was moving in every direction at once, and at some point finding himself outside, crouched behind a parked car, unable to account for how he had gotten there. Three people near the stage were killed. Kofi was physically uninjured, but he did not leave the city for two days, and when he finally drove home, he could not fully explain what had happened in the hours immediately after the explosion. There are portions of that afternoon he has never been able to retrieve, no matter how many times he has tried.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of the event began to return in ways he had not chosen. Without warning — while cutting fabric, while eating, while lying in bed — the blast would replay with a completeness that felt less like remembering and more like reliving: the crack of the explosion, the fence, the crowd pressing against him. At other times, he could recall the same sequence and feel almost nothing, watching it as though it had happened to someone else entirely, a stranger in a story he had only been told. This inconsistency disturbed him as much as the intrusions themselves. He had come to believe that a man who truly had himself together would not be undone this way, and the fact that he was — that he could not control when or how the memory came, or whether it arrived with feeling or without — confirmed something he had begun to suspect about himself: that he was not strong enough, that when it mattered most, he had simply run.

His behaviour in the shop changed in ways his regular customers noticed. He rearranged the layout so that his cutting table sits against the back wall, giving him a clear view of the door and both windows. When a delivery driver enters or a customer arrives unexpectedly, his eyes move to the exits before he registers who has come in. He cannot explain this to anyone in terms that feel adequate, so he does not try. He has stopped attending any event where a crowd might gather — street fairs, church services, even a cousin's graduation — and has quietly withdrawn from most of the social fabric that once sustained him. He has also stopped making any meaningful plans for the business: no new equipment, no lease renewal discussions, no expansion ideas he used to sketch on the back of pattern paper. The future feels like a place he is not entitled to assume he will reach.

In the evenings, he spends long stretches on his phone — games, videos, anything that fills the space where thought would otherwise settle. On some nights, he picks arguments with people online or with his roommate over small things, and afterward he cannot fully account for why he did it. He has come to feel that he does not belong in his community here, nor does he belong back home, nor anywhere in particular.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment in his shop three weeks ago when a car backfired on the street outside and he found himself flat against the back wall, heart hammering, before he had consciously registered what the sound was. A customer was watching him. He made an excuse, finished the fitting, and sat alone afterward for a long time. What he is most afraid of, he said at intake, is that this is simply who he is now. What he is hoping, more quietly, is that it is not.
